pages.x: The Dzungars were western Mongols who had built the last great empire of nomad horsemen, ruling from the Ili valley over the steppes and oases of Central Asia. For seventy years they had fought the Qing emperors of China for the lands between. But when their khan died in 1745, his sons and nobles fought each other for the throne.

In 1754 one of the losers, the noble Amursana, fled to the Qing and asked for help. The Qianlong Emperor saw his chance to end the Dzungar threat for good. In 1755 two Qing armies marched west with Amursana, clan after clan went over to them, and the Dzungar capital in the Ili valley fell almost without a fight.

Amursana had hoped to rule all the Dzungars, but Qianlong split them into four small khanates under his control. That autumn Amursana rose against the Qing. The small garrison left at Ili was wiped out, and its general killed himself. The Qing drove Amursana into the Kazakh steppe, but the Dzungars kept rising.

In 1757 Qianlong ordered that the Dzungars be wiped out. His armies swept the land, killing the men and carrying off women and children as slaves, while smallpox raced through the camps. Amursana fled to Russia and died of smallpox. Of perhaps 600,000 Dzungars, most were killed or died, and many historians call it a genocide.
pages.of: Dzungars killed, dead of disease or fled

pages.x: South of the mountains, the Muslim oasis cities of the Tarim Basin, led by two brothers of a family of holy men, the Khojas, now defied the Qing. Qing armies took Kucha, were themselves trapped for months near Yarkand, then took Kashgar and Yarkand in 1759. The Khojas fled to Badakhshan, where its ruler had them killed.

Qianlong had his victories drawn by the Jesuit painters at his court, among them Giuseppe Castiglione. In 1765 he sent sixteen of their battle scenes to Paris, where the best engravers in Europe cut them into copper plates. The prints, finished by 1775, show tiny Dzungar horsemen scattering before the Qing banners.

The Qing called the conquered lands Xinjiang, the New Frontier, and filled the empty grasslands with soldiers, Han Chinese farmers, Muslims from the oases and Kazakhs. In 1771 the Torghuts, cousins of the Dzungars who had moved to the Volga more than a century before, trekked back across the steppe to settle there, and lost more than half their people on the way.

The conquest gave the Qing a vast new territory and drew borders of China much like those of today. It ended two thousand years in which nomad empires of the steppe had threatened China. But the Dzungars, a whole people, almost vanished, and their name lives on mostly in the Dzungarian Basin.
pts: The last steppe empire was destroyed
Most of the Dzungars died or fled
Xinjiang became part of the Qing empire
